title: Ms. X & The The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
text:
Decision
Ms. X & The The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-161108-Q2C5X0
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the Department was justified in refusing access, under section29(1) of the FOI Act to records of submissions to an interdepartmental consultation process
09 July 2026
Background
The background to this review is the preparation of revised regulations, as part of the phased commencement of the Planning and Development Act 2024 (hereinafter 2024 Act). In February 2025, the Department invited government departments and bodies to make submissions to inform the drafting of updated regulations in relation to Exempted Development and the traffic light approach to Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) screening thresholds. It noted that there would be further opportunity for departments, State bodies and the wider public to make submissions through public consultation. In March 2025, the Department published the related Planning and Development Act 2024 Implementation Plan.
Referencing a specified media article that reported on plans to exempt certain works from planning permission, the applicant submitted a request to the Department for copies of the “ submissions made by the 11 government departments, planning bodies, and local authorities
”.
By decision of 27 June 2025, the Department refused access to all 43 records it identified as coming within the scope of the request under section 29(1) of the FOI Act. It said all of the records are relevant to the deliberative processes underway in relation to the review of exempted development provisions and that pending the conclusion of those deliberative processes, it would be contrary to the public interest to release these records.
On 4 July 2025, the applicant sought an internal review of that decision. On 25 July 2025, the Department affirmed its refusal of the request. On 1 August 2025, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of the Department’s decision. She argued that the Department failed to demonstrate how release of records refused would be contrary to the public interest.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the correspondence outlined above and to the submissions made by the parties. I have also had regard to the contents of the records at issue. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
The Department interpreted the applicant’s request broadly, to cover records of submissions made in response to the invitation to make submissions. Records identified related both to EIA screening thresholds and Exempted Development Regulations. In its correspondence with this Office, the Department said Exempted Development Regulations are set out at Schedule 2 of the Planning and Development Regulations 2001 (as amended). It said the Schedule contains approximately 120 classes of development and is not limited to domestic developments. The Department emphasised that housing policy (including domestic planning exemptions) is under its own remit, and departments were invited to review any classes of exemption applicable to their distinct statutory responsibilities i.e. that they, or bodies under their aegis, considered required amendment. I also note that domestic exempted developments was the main feature of the article linked by the applicant in her FOI request. However, the intended purpose of the Department did not preclude submissions on matters outside the direct remit of the respondent departments and bodies, including housing.
Accordingly, this review is concerned solely with the question of whether the Department was justified in refusing access, under section 29(1) of the FOI Act, to the 43 records it identified as coming within the scope of the request.
Preliminary Matters
Section 18(1) provides, that "if it is practicable to do so", access to an otherwise exempt record shall be granted by preparing a copy, in such form as the head of the public body concerned considers appropriate, of the record with the exempt information removed. Section 18(1) does not apply, however, if the copy provided for thereby would be misleading (section 18(2) refers). It should be noted that the Commissioner takes the view that, generally, neither the definition of a record nor the provisions of section 18 envisage or require the extracting of particular sentences or occasional paragraphs from the remainder of a record for the purpose of granting access to those particular sentences or paragraphs.
Analysis and Findings
Section 29(1)
Section 29(1) provides for the refusal of a request if (a) the record concerned contains matter relating to the deliberative process of an FOI body, including opinions, advice, recommendations and the results of consultations considered by the body for the purpose of those processes, and (b) the body considers that the granting of the request would be contrary to the public interest. These are two independent requirements and the fact that the first is met carries no presumption that the second is met.
Section 29(1)(a)
For section 29(1)(a) to apply, the records must contain matter relating to the ‘deliberative process’ of an FOI body. An FOI body relying on this exemption should identify both the deliberative process concerned and any matter in particular which relates to that process. A deliberative process may be described as a thinking process which informs decision making in FOI bodies. It involves the gathering of information from a variety of sources and weighing or considering carefully all of the information and facts obtained with a view to making a decision or reflecting upon the reasons for or against a particular choice. Thus, it involves the consideration of various matters with a view to making a decision on a particular matter. It would, for example, include some weighing up or evaluation of competing options or the consideration of proposals or courses of action. The fact that a deliberative process exists and is ongoing does not mean that the exemption automatically applies without consideration of all the provisions of section 29. Equally, the fact that a deliberative process is at an end does not mean that the exemption can no longer apply.
In its submissions to this Office the Department said the records were submitted by Government Departments and bodies under their aegis in advance of the general public consultation on exempted development and were in response to the circulation of an issues paper by the Department on 24 February 2025 to all Government Departments. It said the records are related to the Department’s respective policy areas and functions of bodies under their Aegis. It said engagement is still ongoing with these bodies as is the requirement of section 4(3) of the Act of 2024 as any changes to legislation may impact the function of Departments and their bodies.
Section 4(3) of the 2024 Act provides that the Minister shall, before making regulations under the Act, consult with any State authority in which functions vest that he or she considers are connected with the matters to which the proposed regulations relate. The issues paper referenced explains that the 2024 Act was signed into law on 17 October 2024 and that an Implementation Plan which would set out the arrangements to implement a phased commencement of the 2024 Act to facilitate the transition to the new legislation across the planning system had been finalised and would be published shortly. It explains that a key part of the arrangements to commence the 2024 Act is preparation of revised regulations to replace the regulations that underpin the Planning and Development Act 2000, as amended (the 2000 Act). It notes that the existing provisions in the 2000 Act will remain in place until the relevant provisions in the 2024 Act are commenced. It explains that the Department is in the process of preparing these updated regulations and that two key sets of regulations will deal with exempted development and also the proposed introduction of a traffic light approach to setting Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) thresholds. It explains that the aim of the paper is to provide Government Departments (in consultation with State Bodies under their aegis) as well as the local government sector an opportunity to advise the Department of any policies or requirements which may be relevant to the preparation of regulations on exempted development and the proposed introduction of a traffic light approach to setting EIA screening thresholds.
Having considered the Department’s submissions and having examined the records, I accept that the records relate to a deliberative process. I find, therefore, that the requirements of section 29(1)(a) are met. However, that is not the end of the matter as I must also consider whether granting access to the record would be contrary to the public interest, pursuant to section 29(1)(b).
Section 29(1)(b)
The public interest test at section 29(1)(b) is a strong test, requiring the FOI body to show that the granting of the request would be contrary to the public interest, and is stronger than the public interest test in many other sections of the Act, which generally requires that the public interest would, on balance, be better served by granting than by refusing to grant the request. This Office accepts that the FOI Act clearly envisages that there will be cases in which disclosure of the details of an FOI body’s deliberations – whether before or, in some cases, after a decision based on those deliberations has been made – would be against the public interest. However, that is not to say that such disclosure is always, as a matter of principle, against the public interest. Any arguments against release under section 29 should be substantiated and supported by the facts of the case. An FOI body should show how granting access to the particular record would be contrary to the public interest, e.g. by identifying a specific harm to the public interest flowing from release.
Timing of release is relevant to consideration of section 29(1)(b). However, the fact that a deliberative process exists and is ongoing does not mean that the exemption automatically applies. Equally, the fact that a deliberative process is at an end does not mean that the exemption automatically does not apply.
The applicant submitted that an ongoing deliberative process did not equate to an automatic exemption from release and that the Department failed to demonstrate that it would be contrary to the public interest to release the record. She argued that informed public debate about a subject of significant public interest, involving considerations around housing standards and affordability, climate considerations around compact development, is significantly in the public interest. She noted that government ministers have been debating in public the issues under consideration, and she argued that if that doesn't impede the decision-making process, it is hard to see how releasing these documents would.
During the review, this Office’s Investigator sought to clarify the status of the deliberations. The Department submitted that the deliberative process was ongoing in respect of all relevant records. Though its precise submissions varied in relation to the strands of regulatory reform at issue, it was consistent in its position that the deliberative process was ongoing. It said the submissions by Departments and State Bodies relate to policies and functions under the remit of those bodies. It said the possible amendment of planning legislation which could impact and alter the functions of State Bodies requires detailed consideration. It said the process for public scrutiny of Exempted Development legislation is through the Oireachtas which is only finalised once any proposed legislation is approved by both Houses of the Oireachtas. It said the deliberative process is therefore ongoing until the legislation reaches the Oireachtas and said it is inappropriate to provide inaccurate information as engagement is ongoing.
As regards Exempted Development regulations, at the time of its submission the Department said all such regulations were “ at various stages of the drafting process and require screening to determine if a full Strategic Environmental Assessment or Appropriate Assessment is required
.” It said that following environmental assessment, the regulations will “… proceed for formal ratification by resolution of both Houses of the Oireachtas, following referral to the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Housing
.”
Responding to the Investigator’s query regarding a government Press Release of 21 April 2026, titled Government announces changes to Planning Exemptions Regulations which appeared to indicate a concluded deliberative process, it said proposed amendments to domestic/residential exemptions was only one element of the overall exempted development regulations, and residential exemptions were being progressed under the 2000 Act in advance of the commencement of equivalent provisions under the 2024 Act.
During the review, Regulations regarding domestic planning exemptions progressed, and the Department has now clarified that several domestic draft regulations were prioritised and have been referred to the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Housing, Local Government and Heritage for consideration on 14 July 2026. It said it regards the deliberative process as ongoing with respect to these regulations and highlighted that these regulations, relating to housing, are under the Department’s own remit.
As regards EIA regulations, the Department said, at the time of its submission, that a review of the EIA screening thresholds was ongoing, and preparations were being made to progress a public consultation. The Department said it expected the public consultation would be open for submissions in Q2 2026.
The applicant’s submissions regarding the public interest test at section 29 were put to the Department. As to how release of the records at issue would be contrary to the public interest, the Department said it needs appropriate time and space to deliberate and decide on this matter, and it argued that the public interest would not be served by any action that might hinder the Department’s deliberative processes. It said that until a policy or action is agreed between relevant stakeholders, the discussion remains internal. It argued that granting the request would be contrary to the public interest as it may negatively impact on the operation of Departments and State Bodies in the carrying out of their function by providing a false narrative of what may or may not be in final legislation. It said that providing information which is not yet finalised / decided upon may have unintended consequences such as creating an anomaly for certain types of development by either artificially increasing or decreasing the number of planning applications. It said the planning system deals with over 30,000 planning applications annually. It said that only once legislation is approved by the Minister and in the case of Exempted Development, approved by positive resolution of the Houses of the Oireachtas, can it become law. It argued, therefore, that prematurely publishing information contained within the deliberative process may create a false narrative as the deliberative process is not yet finalised.
The Department’s response was requested on the applicant’s submission that the matter was addressed by politicians and covered in the media. The Department made a distinction between the records at issue which concerned other departments and bodies, and its own policies. It said that while some information in relation to certain proposed exemptions has been discussed in the media, this was in relation to policy issues which come under the remit of the Department and do not relate to policies of other government departments or agencies.
Responding to the applicant’s submission that release of the records was in the public interest and would lead to “informed public debate about a subject of significant public interest”, the Department highlighted that public consultation provided an opportunity for private individuals and organisations to make submissions on exempted development, including relating to residential development. The Department clarified that the public consultation (regarding Exempted Development Regulations) yielded approximately 900 submissions, and it is understood that copies will be published to the Government website by 30 September 2026. It restated the distinction between its own policy and submissions.
Analysis
In the course of this analysis, I have had regard to public-facing information. I note that in terms of publication arrangements, there appears to be a material distinction between publication of submissions to public consultation processes as opposed to submissions to an interdepartmental consultation process. The Public Consultation Principles & Guidance of the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation place an emphasis on publication of public consultation responses in order to create a “legislative footprint”. However, I am not aware of any equivalent guidance for publication of submissions to an interdepartmental consultation. The Issues Paper furnished to this Office instructed that government Departments could make additional submissions to a public consultation process, and I note the guidance to both public consultations included that submissions may be published. The Issues Paper and request for submissions to this consultation process did not contain the same points of information as the public consultations as regards potential publication.
I have fully considered the parties’ submissions and the records at issue. I note that Regulations regarding EIA and Exempted Developments are at different stages.
Noting the Department’s submission on the status of EIA Regulations, I consider that the process of regulatory reform is at a relatively early stage. I note that at the time of writing, the public consultation process has only recently closed. Regarding Exempted Development Regulations, my understanding of the Department’s submission is that the regulations are at a more advanced stage relative to EIA regulations. The Department initially submitted that all Exempted Development Regulations are at “ various stages of the drafting process
” and that following drafting and environmental screening/ assessment, the regulations will go before the Oireachtas. As set out above, at the time of writing, some draft regulations will shortly go before an Oireachtas Committee.
The applicant has submitted that the public interest would be served by the release of the records. Section 29(1)(b) does not require me to consider whether the weight of the public interest favouring disclosure of the records is greater than the weight of the public interest favouring the withholding of the records. Rather, it requires that disclosure “would be contrary to the public interest”.
Having considered the parties’ submissions, I accept that the process of policy formation and regulatory reform is complex, that the Department needs appropriate time and space to deliberate and decide on matters, and that any action that might hinder the Department’s deliberative processes is contrary to the public interest.
Insofar as the records relate to EIA Regulations, I accept the Department’s submission that release of records relating to EIA Regulations would be contrary to the public interest. This deliberative process is not only ongoing, but also at a relatively early stage, and I agree that the Department requires space to engage with Departments and bodies.
Insofar as the records relate to Exempted Development Regulations, I consider that drafting and pre-legislative scrutiny are fluid, deliberative processes. While elements of a legislative approach would have been deliberated on in order the inform such processes, I accept the deliberative process is still ongoing. As release of records under FOI is equivalent to their publication to the world at large, I accept that release may hinder this deliberative process. I consider the Department’s submission regarding potential misinformation in the context of planning exemptions, specifically, the potential harm of artificially increasing or decreasing the number of planning applications, to be sufficiently cogent and fact-based to meet the requirements of section 29 (1)(b).
I note that the Department previously stated the deliberative process was ongoing until the legislation reaches the Oireachtas which appears to contradict its subsequent position that the deliberative process is ongoing with respect to regulations shortly before an Oireachtas Committee. However, the Department has clarified that the Oireachtas Committee is a form of pre-legislative scrutiny. I accept this distinction.
In light of the above, I accept that disclosure of the records would be contrary to the public interest. I find that the second requirement of section 29(1), as set out at section 29(1)(b) of the FOI Act, has been met.
Section 29(2) – exceptions
Section 29(2) provides that subsection (1) does not apply to a record if and in so far as it contains any or all of the following:
a) matter such as rules, procedures, guidelines, interpretations and precedents used, or intended to be used, by an FOI body for the purpose of making decisions, determinations or recommendations;
b) factual information;
c) the reasons for the making of a decision by an FOI body;
d) a report of an investigation or analysis of the performance, efficiency or effectiveness of an FOI body in relation to the functions generally or a particular function of the body;
e) a report, study or analysis of a scientific or technical expert relating to the subject of his or her expertise or a report containing opinions or advice of such an expert and not being a report used or commissioned for the purposes of a decision of an FOI body made pursuant to any enactment or scheme.
The applicant submitted that the identified records “likely include "factual information" and analysis, which would make them non-exempt.” The Department was requested to clarify its position as to whether the records contained non-exempt information as specified at section 29(2) of the FOI Act. In response the Department said the submissions consist of issues for discussion, draft material and observations." Having examined the records, I consider they do contain severable factual information as follows:
Record No.
Description of factual information
Record 5
Page 1, paras. 2-3
Record 8
Text under Heading A1, A2 (except final two sentences), A4, text under heading 1, except last sentence, text under heading two, except last sentence.
Record 11
Page 1, paras. 3-4, Page 2, para. 1
Record 15
Page 2, paras. 2 - 3; Page 4, para. 2 (i.e. para. 1 under heading 2.0)
Record 21
Page 1, paras. 2 - 4, 6
Record 22
Pages 1-2, all information at heading 2.0
Record 29
Page 2, Para 1, excluding fist sentence
Record 34
Page 2, all text under sub-heading “introduction”, Page 3, paras. 1-3.
I find section 29(2)(b) applies to the above-specified information. I direct release of same.
Having regard to the remainder of the records, while I accept that the records contain factual information, it is relevant that the factual information is, in other instances inextricably linked to other types of information such as analysis, opinions, etc. I have already outlined the provisions of section 18 of the FOI Act and the Commissioner’s approach to the matter. In my view, it would not be practicable to attempt to further extract any factual information from these records while at the same time ensuring that the redacted copies are not misleading under section 18 of the Act. With respect to these records, I find that section 29(2)(b) does not apply.
Further to the above, I am satisfied that none of the other provisions of section 29(2) apply in this case.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act I hereby vary the decision of the Department. I find that section 29(2)(b) applies to certain specified records as specified in this decision and, I direct release of same. I find that the Department was justified in refusing to release the remainder of records of submissions to a consultation process under section 29(1) of the Act.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated by the requester not later than eight weeks after notice of the decision was given, and by any other party not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given.
Stephen Rafferty
Senior Investigator
respondent: The The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
